ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The pedigree shows three individuals marked with a question mark: individual 2, individual 8, and individual 11. Individual 11 is a circle with a question mark, paired with individual 10, a fully shaded square. Their immediate offspring are individuals 16, 17, and 18. In the image, 16 and 18 are unshaded squares, while 17 is a fully shaded circle. The legend states that each half of a symbol represents one copy of the gene, and shading means the color-blindness allele is present. Reasoning: Since individual 10 is fully shaded, individual 10 contributes a color-blindness allele to offspring. The fully shaded child 17 must have received a color-blindness allele from both parents, so individual 11 must carry the color-blindness allele. However, the unshaded children 16 and 18 require individual 11 to also be able to contribute a normal allele. Therefore, individual 11 has one color-blindness allele and one normal allele, making individual 11 heterozygous. Among the individuals marked with '?', the heterozygous individual is 11.

In the 10×11 family, the father 10 is affected, daughter 17 is affected, and sons 16 and 18 are unaffected. Because an affected daughter needs a color-blindness allele from her mother as well as from her affected father, individual 11 must carry the allele. Because her sons are unaffected, she must also carry a normal allele. Therefore individual 11 is the heterozygous '?' individual.

planner_metadata.knowledge_role: Color blindness is typically X-linked recessive. An affected daughter must inherit a mutant X from both parents; unaffected sons inherit their X from the mother, so their normal status shows the mother has a normal X. Thus the mother of both an affected daughter and unaffected sons must be X^N X^c, i.e. heterozygous.
